summary: Defines an architecture framework and functional requirements for carrying signaling information, such as telephone call setup messages, over IP networks. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Telephone networks use signaling messages to set up and manage calls. This RFC describes the roles and transport requirements for carrying those messages across Internet Protocol (IP) networks.

questions: how to transport signaling over ip
how is ss7 carried over ip
what is a media gateway controller
subtitle: A framework for carrying telephone-network signaling messages over IP.

tldr.problem: Telephone signaling protocols need defined roles, interfaces, and performance expectations when carried over IP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes gateway functions, a three-part signaling transport stack, and requirements based on existing circuit-network protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational architecture and requirements document, not a signaling transport protocol.

today: RFC 2719 is an Informational framework from October 1999, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets architecture and requirements rather than defining the signaling transport protocol.

sections.title: Scope of Signaling Transport
sections.content:
Signaling Transport (SIG) is a protocol stack for carrying message-based signaling from a Switched Circuit Network (SCN) over Internet Protocol (IP). Its job is transparent transport: it carries the SCN messages without defining the SCN protocols or translating them.

The framework applies between a Signaling Gateway Unit and a Media Gateway Controller Unit. It may also be used between other gateway or controller entities when their signaling needs it.
sections.plainLanguage: SIG carries call-control messages from telephone networks across IP. It transports the messages; it does not translate or redefine them.

sections.title: Gateway Roles
sections.content:
A Signaling Gateway receives or sends native circuit-network signaling at the edge of an IP network. A Media Gateway Controller manages media-gateway resources and can terminate or originate signaling protocols.

A Media Gateway terminates circuit-network media streams and packetizes them for a packet network. These functions may run in separate physical units or be combined. The RFC shows examples for SS7, ISDN, and database access.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework separates signaling reception, call control, and media handling into roles. A network can place those roles in separate devices or combine them.

sections.title: The Signaling Transport Stack
sections.content:
SIG is described as three components: an adaptation sub-layer for the needs of a particular circuit-network application, a common signaling transport protocol for shared reliable functions, and a standard IP transport protocol underneath.

The architecture examples show how this stack can carry SS7 layers, ISDN Q.931 signaling, or signaling between gateways. The framework does not define the protocol formats for these components.
sections.plainLanguage: The stack adapts a particular phone signaling protocol, adds common transport functions, and uses IP below them. The RFC defines the structure, not the wire protocol.

sections.title: Functional and Performance Requirements
sections.content:
SIG must identify which circuit-network protocol it carries and provide a common base protocol that can be extended. Depending on that protocol, it may need flow control, in-sequence delivery within a control stream, error detection, retransmission, failure recovery, and detection of unavailable peers.

The RFC derives performance targets from existing signaling systems. Examples include MTP Level 3 peer responses within 500 to 1200 milliseconds, route-set availability of 99.9998% or better, and a Q.931 round-trip delay that should not exceed 4 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Call-control messages need reliable delivery and timing that respects the phone protocols they already use. The RFC records example limits from those protocols.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
Operations and management of IP or circuit networks are outside the SIG scope. For signaling carried only inside an intranet, the network owner chooses the security measures. Signaling that crosses the public Internet should be treated as exposed to risk.

The RFC identifies authentication, integrity, availability, and sometimes confidentiality as security needs. It recommends IPsec or an equivalent existing mechanism rather than defining new security mechanisms for SIG.
sections.plainLanguage: Signaling over the public Internet needs protection against forgery, changes, and outages. The RFC recommends using existing security mechanisms.
